title: PVC and CPVC Cement: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) Hazards
summary: Many PVC and CPVC primers and cements contain tetrahydrofuran (THF), which is believed to cause cancer with long exposure. Check labels, wear the right PPE, store it safely, and ask for safer products.
talking_points: THF is a common solvent in these products at 10 percent to 70 percent. Most products contain at least some. Long-term exposure to THF is believed to cause cancer, based on kidney and liver cancer in animal studies.
THF evaporates quickly while primer and cement dry and gets in the air. You can be exposed by breathing it in or by skin contact.
Check the label and the safety data sheet for "tetrahydrofuran," "THF," or "oxolane." Look for the OSHA health hazard pictogram or a California Proposition 65 warning.
Ask for safer products. Several products on the market do not contain THF and perform about the same and meet the applicable standards.
Wear the PPE your employer provides. Check the label and Section 8 of the safety data sheet for the right respiratory protection, eye protection, and gloves.
Do not use cloth gloves. They absorb the solvent and hold it against your skin. Use chemical-resistant gloves such as nitrile, and wash cement off your skin right away with soap and water.
Get training on handling and storage before you work with these products.

Store them away from oxidizing agents, such as chlorine, hydrogen peroxide, nitric acid, and bleach, because violent reactions can occur. Keep them in tightly closed containers in a cool, well-ventilated area, away from smoking and open flames.
site_hazards_to_check: PVC or CPVC cement with THF stored in warm or poorly ventilated areas
Workers using cloth gloves with cement
No respiratory protection, eye protection, or chemical-resistant gloves
Cement stored near bleach, cleaners, disinfectants, or other oxidizers
Open cement containers or containers near ignition sources
No safety data sheet or label check for the product in use
discussion_questions: Does the cement we are using contain THF, and how do we know?
What gloves and respirator does the safety data sheet call for?
Could we switch to a product without THF for this job?
